description: From medieval miasma to modern epidemiology — what caused disease, and how ideas changed.
content_html:
Understanding Disease: A Changing Picture

For most of human history, people had no way of observing the microscopic world. Without the ability to see bacteria or viruses, explanations for disease had to come from observation, tradition and belief. Over 1,500 years, ideas about the causes of illness shifted dramatically — from supernatural forces and bad air to the germ theory that underpins modern medicine.

Medieval Ideas: Miasma, God and the Humours

In medieval Britain (c.500–1500), illness was explained in three main ways. First, many believed that miasma — foul-smelling air produced by decay — entered the body and caused sickness. Towns with open sewers and rotting rubbish were thought to be particularly dangerous, not because of germs but because of the smell itself.

Second, disease was widely seen as divine punishment. If a community sinned, God might send plague or pestilence as a warning or judgement. This belief meant that prayer, fasting and confession were considered as important as any physical remedy. Third, the theory of the four humours explained illness as an imbalance in the body’s fluids. Physicians tried to restore balance through bleeding, purging and adjusting diet.

Key Fact

Medieval people explained illness through miasma (bad air), divine punishment (God’s will) and the theory of the four humours (imbalance of bodily fluids). None of these explanations involved germs or infection in the modern sense.

The Black Death, 1348

The Black Death arrived in England in 1348, killing approximately one third of the population within three years. People had no way of knowing that the disease was spread by fleas carried on rats, or that it was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Instead, they blamed miasma, divine punishment, or the position of the planets. The responses this produced — burning herbs, flagellation, quarantine of towns — were based entirely on these mistaken beliefs. Quarantine, however, did accidentally help slow the spread in some communities.

The Great Plague of 1665 was the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in England, killing around 100,000 people in London alone — roughly a quarter of the city’s population. Despite being three centuries after the Black Death, the explanations offered were still largely the same: miasma and divine punishment. Physicians wore beak-shaped masks filled with aromatic herbs, believing this would filter out the bad air. The plague orders issued by the authorities ordered the killing of cats and dogs (which may have made things worse by removing some natural rat predators) and the lighting of fires in streets to ‘purify’ the air. The underlying belief — that foul smells caused disease — had barely changed.

Industrialisation and New Disease Challenges

The Industrial Revolution of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries created new threats to health. Rapid urban growth meant that thousands of people were crowded into slums with inadequate sewage systems and contaminated water supplies. Diseases such as cholera and typhoid thrived in these conditions.

Cholera first struck Britain in 1831–1832 and returned in 1848–1849 and 1853–1854. Typhoid was endemic in Victorian towns. Many educated people — including leading doctors — still blamed miasma. The smell from sewage and the Thames was blamed for the epidemics. This was wrong in its cause but accidentally correct in its consequence: cleaning up smells did sometimes mean cleaning up water, which genuinely stopped disease.

Key Fact

Industrialisation created overcrowded towns with poor sanitation, contaminated water and inadequate sewers. Cholera epidemics struck in 1831, 1848 and 1853. These conditions made urban disease far more deadly than in rural medieval England.

The decisive shift came when Louis Pasteur published his germ theory in 1861, demonstrating that microorganisms caused fermentation and decay. Robert Koch built on this between the 1870s and 1890s, identifying specific bacteria as the causes of specific diseases — including anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883). This was a revolution: for the first time, a scientific mechanism for how disease spread had been identified. Miasma was no longer just insufficient — it was demonstrably wrong.

Twentieth-Century Understanding: Bacteria, Viruses and Beyond

By the early twentieth century, scientists understood that diseases were caused either by bacteria (such as tuberculosis or cholera) or by viruses (such as influenza or smallpox). The 1918 influenza pandemic killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people worldwide — more than the First World War — demonstrating that even with improved knowledge, disease could still be catastrophic.

Later in the century, new diseases challenged the medical world. HIV/AIDS was first identified in 1981 and spread globally within years, caused by a retrovirus transmitted through blood and bodily fluids. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, emerged in late 2019 and became a global pandemic in 2020. Both diseases showed that new pathogens can emerge and spread rapidly even when medical science is highly advanced. Modern epidemiology tracks and analyses disease patterns across populations, enabling faster responses than were ever possible in medieval or even Victorian times.
exam_tip_html: On questions asking you to explain a cause or consequence, be specific about the time period — the examiner wants to see you distinguish between medieval, early modern and modern explanations. Don’t just say ‘people believed in miasma’: say when, give an example of how it shaped behaviour (such as the beaked masks in 1665), and explain why this view persisted. For 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ questions, you must show the change over time and link it to a factor such as science, technology or government action.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval explanations for disease centred on miasma, divine punishment and the theory of the four humours; none recognised infection by microorganisms.
  • Industrialisation created new disease threats through overcrowding and contaminated water; cholera epidemics struck Britain in 1831, 1848 and 1853.
  • Germ theory (Pasteur, 1861; Koch, 1870s–1890s) replaced miasma as the scientific explanation for disease, transforming how medicine understood and eventually fought illness.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of medieval beliefs about the causes of disease.
practice_questions.marks: One feature, supported with accurate detail. Example: People believed disease was caused by miasma (bad air), thought to rise from rotting matter and sewage. This led them to burn herbs or light fires to purify the air. [2 marks: 1 for identifying a feature, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of industrialisation on disease in nineteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Rapid urbanisation created overcrowded slums with contaminated water supplies, enabling diseases like cholera and typhoid to spread quickly. Feature 2: Poor sewage disposal in industrial towns meant waste polluted rivers and drinking water, leading to multiple cholera epidemics (1831, 1848, 1853). [2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the persistence of the miasma theory in Britain into the nineteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: Clear identification of a cause (e.g. lack of microscopes / no awareness of microorganisms) with sustained explanation of why this allowed miasma to go unchallenged. Developing: A cause is identified but explanation is limited. Emerging: A simple statement about miasma without explanation of why it persisted. [6 marks — Mastering: sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and clear link to change; Secure: clear cause with relevant evidence; Developing: some explanation, limited evidence; Emerging: simple points, little evidence]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of germ theory for understanding disease in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (overturned miasma, gave basis for targeted treatments, enabled public health reform) AND over time (antibiotics, vaccines, modern epidemiology). Secure: Significance at the time covered with relevant evidence; some reference to longer-term impact. Developing: One aspect of significance with limited evidence. Emerging: Simple statement about Pasteur or Koch without analysis. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Miasma theory was the most important reason why disease was difficult to control in Britain before 1900.'
How far do you agree with this statement? Use your knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument evaluating miasma alongside other factors (poverty, lack of government action, rapid urbanisation, religious beliefs) with a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Both sides addressed with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion. Developing: Some discussion of miasma and one other factor, limited judgement. Emerging: Description of miasma only, no weighing of factors. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How has the understanding of the causes of disease changed between the medieval period and the present day? Use evidence across all three eras to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across all three eras (medieval: miasma/humours/God; early modern: miasma persists through 1665; modern: germ theory to virology), weighs change against continuity, reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: All three eras covered with evidence, clear line of argument. Developing: Two eras covered; limited weighing of change vs continuity. Emerging: Single-era narrative, no comparative judgement. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which theory claimed that disease was caused by an imbalance of bodily fluids?
options: The theory of the four humours

knowledge_checks.q: Which scientist first identified specific bacteria as the causes of specific diseases in the 1870s–1890s?
The Black Death arrived in England in _____, killing approximately one third of the population.
Cholera and typhoid spread rapidly in industrial towns because of contaminated _____ supplies.
Match each theory of disease to its main cause:
right: Bad air from rotting matter causes illness
Illness results from an imbalance of bodily fluids

flashcard_questions.q: What was the miasma theory of disease?
flashcard_questions.a: The belief that disease was caused by bad air rising from rotting matter and waste.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the three main medieval explanations for the cause of disease?
flashcard_questions.a: Miasma, divine punishment and the theory of the four humours.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Black Death arrive in England?
Approximately what fraction of England's population died in the Black Death?
When did the Great Plague devastate London, killing around 100,000 people?
What did the theory of the four humours claim caused illness?
flashcard_questions.a: An imbalance among blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

flashcard_questions.q: In which year did Louis Pasteur publish his germ theory?
Robert Koch identified the bacterium causing tuberculosis in which year?
How did industrialisation increase disease in nineteenth-century British towns?
flashcard_questions.a: Overcrowding and contaminated water supplies spread cholera and typhoid.

flashcard_questions.q: In which year did the first major cholera epidemic strike Britain?
flashcard_questions.a: 1831, when cholera arrived from the Continent and swept through industrial towns.

flashcard_questions.q: HIV/AIDS was first identified in which year?

flashcard_questions.a: How diseases spread, their causes, and how they can be controlled in populations.

glossary_terms.definition: The theory that disease was caused by bad air rising from rotting matter, waste and swamps.
An ancient theory that the body contained four liquids — blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile — and that illness resulted from an imbalance among them.
The rapid process of economic and social change in the late 18th and 19th centuries by which Britain transformed from a largely agricultural society into one dominated by industry and towns.
An infectious disease spread through contaminated water, causing severe diarrhoea and dehydration, capable of killing within hours.
The scientific study of how diseases spread, their causes, and how they can be controlled in populations.
